title: JavaScript interop and gradual adoption
hook: TypeScript was designed to adopt JavaScript projects incrementally — rename files, loosen checks where needed, and tighten over time. Because types erase, your compiled output can call any JavaScript library without a special bridge, unlike calling native code from C# through Platform Invoke (P/Invoke).

blocks.text: JavaScript interop means TypeScript and JavaScript files coexist in one project. allowJs lets .js files participate in type checking; checkJs adds checking to JS via JSDoc. Declaration files (.d.ts) describe untyped npm packages. @ts-ignore and // @ts-expect-error are escape hatches — use sparingly. Gradual adoption: start with allowJs and noImplicitAny: false on legacy folders, then enable strict per directory. C# interop with JavaScript usually means separate processes (Node + .NET) or hosting engines — not file-by-file mixing in one compile unit.

entries.plainDefinition: Lets JavaScript files be part of the TypeScript program for mixed projects.
entries.example: Legacy src/legacy/*.js imports new src/utils.ts code.

entries.plainDefinition: A file that describes types for JavaScript code without implementing them.
entries.example: @types/lodash provides typings for the lodash package.

entries.plainDefinition: Adding types incrementally instead of converting an entire codebase at once.
entries.example: Migrate one module per sprint from .js to .ts with strict checks.

blocks.text: Most real codebases mix .ts and .js during migration. npm ecosystems ship JavaScript — TypeScript consumes them via types from DefinitelyTyped (@types/*) or bundled .d.ts. Misconfigured interop causes implicit any, duplicate identifiers, and broken imports. For polyglot systems, the TypeScript front end and C# API share HTTP/JSON contracts — not shared source files. Understanding interop keeps brownfield migrations and third-party library usage safe.

blocks.title: Interview one-liner
blocks.body: TS erases to JS — interop is calling the same functions. Use .d.ts for untyped libs, allowJs for legacy files, strict per folder as you migrate. C# ↔ JS is service boundaries, not mixed compilation.

items.title: Add tsconfig with allowJs
items.body: Include existing .js files. Start with loose strictness if needed.

items.title: Rename hot paths to .ts
items.body: Convert high-churn modules first. Add types at boundaries.

items.title: Install @types or write .d.ts
items.body: Cover critical npm dependencies without rewriting them.

items.title: Tighten strict per package
items.body: Enable strict in tsconfig for migrated folders; leave legacy overrides.

items.title: Remove escape hatches
items.body: Replace @ts-ignore with proper types or // @ts-expect-error with tickets.

diagram.title: Mixed JS/TS project structure
diagram.source:
flowchart TD

  LEGACY --> TSC

snippet.label: Legacy JavaScript module
snippet.explanation: Unchanged JS can stay in the repo. TypeScript imports it when allowJs is true; types may be implicit any until you add JSDoc or a .d.ts shim.

snippet.label: TypeScript consumer with declaration shim
snippet.explanation: Ambient module declarations give types without converting the JS file. Similar to extern declarations in C for native libs — describe the surface, implementation stays JS.

snippet.label: JSDoc-typed JavaScript (checkJs)
snippet.explanation: With checkJs: true, tsc validates JSDoc in .js files. Teams can defer .ts rename while still getting type errors in CI.

snippet.label: Untyped npm package — declare module
snippet.explanation: When no types exist, you author minimal .d.ts. Production teams contribute fixes upstream or wrap the library in a typed facade.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Sprinkling @ts-ignore instead of fixing types. Using any for all legacy imports — wrap with unknown + guards at boundaries. Forgetting to add .js extension in ESM relative imports when module is NodeNext. Assuming @types versions always match the runtime package version.

blocks.text: moduleResolution nodenext vs bundler affects how .js interop paths resolve. TypeScript 5+ allowImportingTsExtensions is for type-aware bundlers only. For monorepos, path mapping in tsconfig must match the bundler and test runner. C# Blazor and Jint host JS in-process — rare compared to REST between Node and .NET. Migration metrics: track implicit any count, @ts-expect-error inventory, and strict subproject coverage. esModuleInterop and allowSyntheticDefaultImports smooth CommonJS default import ergonomics.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying TypeScript cannot use JavaScript libraries. Using any everywhere in migration with no plan. Not knowing what .d.ts is for. Claiming C# and TS files compile together in one project like allowJs.

interviewTakeaways: allowJs and checkJs enable incremental migration; types erase so JS and TS share the same run time.
.d.ts and @types/* describe JavaScript packages to the type checker without changing their source.
C# ↔ JavaScript interop is cross-process or hosted engines — not the same as .ts calling .js.
60s: Rename to .ts over time. allowJs for legacy. .d.ts for untyped npm. strict per folder. Polyglot with C# uses JSON/OpenAPI, not mixed compilation.
Follow-up: how do you type a CommonJS default export under NodeNext?
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'We @ts-ignore legacy code.' Strong: 'Shim .d.ts, JSDoc checkJs, migrate hot paths, track expect-error debt.'
Missing .js extension in ESM relative imports under NodeNext.
Strong answer: 'Interop is erased JS calls. Types via declarations. C# boundary is HTTP/schema, not allowJs.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: Interop settings (esModuleInterop, module NodeNext) must match how the JavaScript package exports its API.
.d.ts describes JS to the checker only — same erasure model, types never load at run time.
